![Biological Factors Influence Alcohol Intoxication–A Focus on ...](https://api.dataforseo.com/cdn/i/11230929-1853-0139-0000-d603a8d00bd8:4)
Alcohol is metabolized **primarily in the liver** , which breaks down more than 90% of the ethanol you consume. Small amounts are also broken down in other tissues, such as the gastrointestinal tract, brain, and pancreas.⁠National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) (.gov) +1[[1]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAESdQHEIkXXH28-wrfAon-NJqt5Ug0I4tCDhecqtGjA4qSjtS67iGnkiOKioOamE74aMUI2MMeXnsTl3q-XNengyNwHUGlUUtbrAnMBX_QPC0Sz5W9L_3JZk2COMjnplCzBAnYbAChlFvNUS5rg1bi184MaCPSJLw)[[2]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAESbAHEIkXXRbc6cRjscYA0jf1zubVl-kIEW6YzkgLkcii5pShxPQgO6_0vAmgDvIRXtHMMubZD2QKIAp6jXikitG4YhxV8VBPg_hNn2T8mo4ah6xHrfJJeS6Dtngwe_ff9SMcDuhK5HB4W2PKJsw)

### How It Happens by Location

- **Liver (Primary Site):** After alcohol is absorbed through the stomach and small intestine, blood carries it straight to the liver. Enzymes—mainly **alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)** and **aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH)** —convert ethanol into toxic acetaldehyde, then into acetate. At high alcohol levels or in heavy drinkers, enzymes like **CYP2E1** also help break it down.⁠National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov) +2[[1]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHEIkXXbnuLVFL6a46q3DB_v0syk3hztRecORvMqMObHw72TXUTKRV4ex8SHnvSKOxUs7sEFwKMr51jFqagrVokAS0IZDTJMB1130V5lUfVeEKjtYe-sQYFWrJ5K8aKlpKVkfJr-p9u4QDgeRY)[[2]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAESdQHEIkXXH28-wrfAon-NJqt5Ug0I4tCDhecqtGjA4qSjtS67iGnkiOKioOamE74aMUI2MMeXnsTl3q-XNengyNwHUGlUUtbrAnMBX_QPC0Sz5W9L_3JZk2COMjnplCzBAnYbAChlFvNUS5rg1bi184MaCPSJLw)[[3]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAESbAHEIkXXRbc6cRjscYA0jf1zubVl-kIEW6YzkgLkcii5pShxPQgO6_0vAmgDvIRXtHMMubZD2QKIAp6jXikitG4YhxV8VBPg_hNn2T8mo4ah6xHrfJJeS6Dtngwe_ff9SMcDuhK5HB4W2PKJsw)
- **Gastrointestinal Tract (Stomach and Intestines):** A small fraction of alcohol begins breaking down in the stomach lining and digestive tract before reaching the bloodstream.⁠National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov) +2[[1]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHEIkXXbnuLVFL6a46q3DB_v0syk3hztRecORvMqMObHw72TXUTKRV4ex8SHnvSKOxUs7sEFwKMr51jFqagrVokAS0IZDTJMB1130V5lUfVeEKjtYe-sQYFWrJ5K8aKlpKVkfJr-p9u4QDgeRY)[[2]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAESdQHEIkXXH28-wrfAon-NJqt5Ug0I4tCDhecqtGjA4qSjtS67iGnkiOKioOamE74aMUI2MMeXnsTl3q-XNengyNwHUGlUUtbrAnMBX_QPC0Sz5W9L_3JZk2COMjnplCzBAnYbAChlFvNUS5rg1bi184MaCPSJLw)[[3]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=txNISaSN9OM&t=83)
- **Other Tissues (Brain, Pancreas, and Peripheral Tissues):** Minor amounts of alcohol metabolism occur in organs like the brain and pancreas. Acetate produced in the liver is mostly released into the bloodstream and broken down into carbon dioxide and water mainly outside the liver.⁠ScienceDirect.com  +1[[1]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAESfwHEIkXXMoFgQJ9sgMHyaOmZDmajLai80SiR5FEMqgWU44pQRnREXtmz9yslm1u4BcPYhejQPC0wqoJpByD0M6k75qOLh_ZS4EOurJwyywXS47ByLfdteq-Pq1znPu2OQY0GCQb91cIfW15z45GdRcU-c2_2CmHHJESUGJh2o70)[[2]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAESdQHEIkXXH28-wrfAon-NJqt5Ug0I4tCDhecqtGjA4qSjtS67iGnkiOKioOamE74aMUI2MMeXnsTl3q-XNengyNwHUGlUUtbrAnMBX_QPC0Sz5W9L_3JZk2COMjnplCzBAnYbAChlFvNUS5rg1bi184MaCPSJLw)
- **Elimination Without Metabolism:** Roughly 2% to 10% of alcohol is not metabolized at all and leaves the body unchanged through breath, urine, and sweat.⁠National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov) +1[[1]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAESbAHEIkXXRbc6cRjscYA0jf1zubVl-kIEW6YzkgLkcii5pShxPQgO6_0vAmgDvIRXtHMMubZD2QKIAp6jXikitG4YhxV8VBPg_hNn2T8mo4ah6xHrfJJeS6Dtngwe_ff9SMcDuhK5HB4W2PKJsw)[[2]](https://google.com/goto?url=CAEScQHEIkXXQz7A3opo8CE3hyaYWASVnCt4NZELSUdE5PN1zKoD3yEJo6clsT43woFiH7rb9n_UKNT0T7sR7NHncFQ4F_8GcasJCeqAPzre08AFb0HYDfk9yT9tgorm5W2mJpglWXUK4L0GPsL0nH0I2kTr)

items.text: Liver (Primary Site): After alcohol is absorbed through the stomach and small intestine, blood carries it straight to the liver. Enzymes—mainly alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) and aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) —convert ethanol into toxic acetaldehyde, then into acetate. At high alcohol levels or in heavy drinkers, enzymes like CYP2E1 also help break it down. Gastrointestinal Tract (Stomach and Intestines): A small fraction of alcohol begins breaking down in the stomach lining and digestive tract before reaching the bloodstream. Other Tissues (Brain, Pancreas, and Peripheral Tissues): Minor amounts of alcohol metabolism occur in organs like the brain and pancreas. Acetate produced in the liver is mostly released into the bloodstream and broken down into carbon dioxide and water mainly outside the liver. Elimination Without Metabolism: Roughly 2% to 10% of alcohol is not metabolized at all and leaves the body unchanged through breath, urine, and sweat.
